prospect.name: Den Keo
prospect.occupation: Service manager for a medical company. Works in the field with his team and remotely from home, and travels roughly one week in every three to four. Has taken on a second job to service a mortgage — 'when you're in California, you got to work two jobs to buy a house out here.'
prospect.family_status: Married; a four-year-old daughter who currently sleeps in their bed; planning another child next year. The youngest of several siblings, all two to four years older. Parents and sisters are described as not interested in fitness and as managing type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure on medication.
prospect.training_background: A long-term consistent trainer who describes himself as plateaued and comfortable. Runs traditional body-part splits — 'Today's Monday, so I'm like, okay, I'm gonna do chest and tris today' — at a 24 Hour Fitness he uses while travelling. Prefers a commercial gym for the social aspect and says a home gym killed his motivation. Does a dynamic warm-up but has stopped post-workout stretching and foam rolling, citing time. Around 8,000 steps a day. Played three sports year-round in high school at about 135 lb. Reads longevity research and cites VO2 max as a priority. Does not drink.
prospect.medical: An old left knee injury that was never treated — 'the only thing I have is like this less knee injury from a long time ago, but, you know, I never got it fixed.' It is not painful but produces instability under unilateral load: 'let's say Bulgarian split squat, I can feel instability... and then the muscles just, I have, like, an imbalance', to the point he does single-leg leg extensions to compensate. Associated hip tightness and reduced squat depth: 'I used to be able to get as the grass on my squats, really easy, and now it feels I have to do a little bit more work to get there.' Sleep is disrupted by his daughter sharing the bed. Strong family history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension across parents and siblings. No clinician has assessed the knee at any point.

signals: Textbook good-to-great language throughout: 'I'm still not in the best shape of my life', 'there's no growth anymore', 'plateau and maybe just comfort'
Already fit and consistent — years of training, meal prep on Sundays, 8,000 steps, no alcohol, no sweet tooth, reads VO2 max research

Frames fitness as the last unfinished item in an otherwise successful life: 'my faith, my family, and then my fitness. So that's like the three Fs of my life. And now that I have my faith and my family are pretty solid. Fitness is the last pillar'
The rep named the avatar correctly out loud and got agreement: 'you're not in a really bad spot, you're just, from what I'm hearing, you want to just level up, right?' / 'Yep.'

Confidence held at 0.6 because he fails the avatar's defining commercial test. For the_optimizer price is meant to be a quality signal rather than a barrier; here it was an absolute barrier — no cash after a $300,000 house deposit, unable to fund even the first $1,200 instalment, and closed only via twelve-month third-party credit taken out on the call.

objections.raw_quote: Okay, 6K, and is there any way I can make monthly payments on that plan, like every month, I complete, it's like another $1,000.
objections.rep_response: Answered with 'Do you need a payment plan?', which produced a full unprompted financial disclosure. Then ran the value isolate — 'just to triple check, like finances aside, does this thing check off all the boxes for you' — and moved directly to structures: split in half with no interest, or six payments of $1,200.

objections.raw_quote: Well, do I have to put in the 1,200 first before we do the 1-on-1, Trevor? Because if so, I'd probably wait another two weeks to get my next paycheck, and then I can put in that 1,200. So maybe let's look out two to three weeks from now for that.
objections.rep_response: Confirmed the first payment was due immediately, established the prospect did not have $1,200 available, and then introduced third-party financing: 'we have the third-party financing option too, like Klarna... You can even split it into 12 months if you want.' No timing play was run.

offer.payment_plan_terms: Four structures appeared. Pay in full at $6,000. Split in half, framed as the interest-free route: 'ideally, like for you to not get any interest on that would be splitting it in half. Is that something that you could do?' Six monthly payments of $1,200, totalling $7,200 — and to the rep's credit the uplift was surfaced, because the prospect spotted it himself: 'so we're adding an extra 200?' / 'Yeah.' The prospect verbally agreed to that route ('So you want to do the six times 1,200?' / 'Yep. Yep.'), then disclosed he could not fund the first instalment, at which point the rep introduced Klarna third-party financing with terms up to twelve months. The prospect applied live, was approved, added a card and completed the first payment, selecting the twelve-month plan. The only figure he cited for it was $662 a month — 'does that mean like I'm paying them the 662 every month, not you guys' — which over twelve months implies roughly $7,944. The rep never stated, confirmed or explained that total, the interest, or the difference from $6,000.
offer.guarantee_mentioned: Stated accurately and in full: 'Trevor guarantees, like there's a guarantee on this six months transformation that within six months, will add eight kilos, which is around 18 pounds to your baseline kettlebell weight on the core movements, like for example, the swing. So for example, if you start with an 8 kilo swing, you will end up with a 16 kilo, at least.' And: 'If you won't hit that in six months, and you will be doing everything as he says, like he will work with you for free, until you do.' Note the prospect immediately observed he already swings 16 kg two-handed, which means the guarantee for him starts from a materially higher baseline than the rep's worked example.

prospect_financials.note: All volunteered rather than asked for. 'I do, just because we bought a house, so I spent literally $300,000 on my own cash for a down payment. So anyways, I don't have any cash, but I just picked up a second job, so I definitely have an extra... about 2,400 extra, which half of it I need to use towards my mortgage, but I definitely can set aside $1,000 every month.' Confirmed he could not produce $1,200 on the day. On credit: 'I checked my FICO this morning... I think we came back with 7.06... Because I had a couple of collections that were, like I was fighting a couple of collections last year. I spent the last year doing credit repairs. I think I'm back in the 700s, like literally this morning.' No question was asked about cards, available credit or investments.

evidence: Third-party financing approved and the first payment completed live: 'congrats, you are approved', 'Add a card to complete your payment', 'Oh, yeah. Okay, there we go. All right, it worked', and the rep confirming 'Oh, okay. Now I see it.'
Prospect confirmed the twelve-month term when asked: 'Which plan did you choose?' / '12 months.'

Clear verbal commitment obtained before the price: 'if we can figure out all the details, like logistical part, are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work?' / 'Yeah. Accountability is a big thing, and that's 100% on me.'

Counter-evidence on completeness: the onboarding call with Trevor was NOT booked. The prospect was in his car without his work schedule and the rep deferred it to a WhatsApp exchange later that morning.
Counter-evidence on completeness: the agreement was never mentioned at any point, and neither was the welcome email, the Skool community or the onboarding questionnaire.
Counter-evidence on what was bought: the amount financed was never stated by the rep, so the sum the prospect is contracted to pay is not established anywhere on the recording.
outcome.next_step: Rep to text on WhatsApp and call back within the hour to book the Trevor onboarding session once the prospect has his work laptop and schedule. Agreement, welcome email, Skool link and onboarding questionnaire all still outstanding.
outcome.cash_collected_note: DERIVED, NOT STATED. The figure is the prospect's single reference to '$662 every month' multiplied by the twelve-month term he confirmed choosing. The rep never spoke a total. The last structure verbally agreed before financing was introduced was six payments of $1,200, totalling $7,200. Both figures exceed the $6,000 stated price. Reconcile against payment records before using this in any cash rollup.

notable.note: The best discovery in the batch attached to the most financially aggressive close in it. Phases 2, 3 and 6 were run properly — the why question at 00:04:52, the two-stage 'what becomes possible' probe, the reflect-back that produced 'I never looked at it that way', and a genuine belief-and-commitment check before any number. Then the money conversation: the prospect disclosed he had put $300,000 cash into a house deposit, had no cash left, had taken a second job of which half is committed to the mortgage, could not fund a $1,200 first instalment, and had spent the previous year repairing his credit while fighting collections. The rep's response was to open a twelve-month consumer credit line on the call. In the sales team meeting recorded the same day this call was reviewed by the whole team, described by a colleague as 'a really phenomenal call' and by the manager as 'That's it, baby' — with the manager's only criticism being that the rep offered payment options instead of running the open wallet first. Also unaddressed: an old knee injury the prospect says was never fixed, which still produces instability and imbalance under single-leg load, on a man now being progressed toward double kettlebell snatches. The rep's response to it was to note that 'there are a lot of PTs that are sometimes working with kettlebells, but from what I saw, what they're doing, it's not so good.'

quality.notes: Heavy inversion throughout, including in the commercially decisive passages. Long blocks carry both speakers under one label with no turn boundaries — 00:02:06-00:03:07, 00:29:27-00:31:00 (the whole nutrition pillar plus the prospect's replies), 00:39:36-00:40:13 and 00:43:24-00:44:01, the last of which contains the prospect's request to delay two to three weeks sitting under the rep's label. The prospect's own name is uncertain: the Fathom label reads 'Den Keo', he refers to an email of 'denysk6@gmail', and the sales team meeting the same day discusses this call as 'Dan Keogh'. Recorded here as the label spells it; a human should reconcile the identity before it is used downstream. There is also a brief video dropout at 00:21:55 and a long silent gap from 00:45:59 to 00:48:35 while the financing application was completed off-audio.
